content.title: About
content.content: Cauliflower is a cruciferous vegetable harvested from the flower heads of Brassica oleracea var. botrytis. When cooked with added fat, it retains a tender texture and gains a richer, buttery flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cauliflower is high in vitamin C, vitamin K, and folate.
There are several varieties: white, green (broccoflower) and purple.
Sautéing with oil creates a golden crust that enhances taste.
Cauliflower can be used as a low‑carb substitute for rice or potatoes when riced.
Historically, cauliflower symbolized purity and was used in ceremonial dishes.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Compounds like glucoraphanin help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Vitamin K and calcium contribute to bone mineralization.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: With moderate fat addition, the dish remains relatively low‑calorie.

items.title: Cruciferous allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to cruciferous vegetables.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: High oxalate intake can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Using large amounts of oil can make the dish calorie‑dense and increase saturated fat intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté, steam, or roast cauliflower with a modest amount of oil (olive, sunflower, etc.). Add herbs, garlic, or lemon juice for extra flavor. Serve as a side dish with meat, fish, or mixed into vegetable medleys.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh cauliflower in the refrigerator in an airtight container or bag for up to 5 days. Cooked cauliflower with oil should be consumed within 2‑3 days, stored in the fridge.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit juice NFS (4075) is a ready‑to‑drink beverage made from a blend of selected fruits. The juice contains no added sugar, preservatives or artificial flavors, preserving the natural taste and aroma of the fruits.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The juice is produced from 100 % natural fruits, without any concentrate.
Each batch undergoes strict quality control and is tested for vitamin content.
It includes fruits rich in vitamin C such as orange, kiwi and strawberry.
Packaging is made from recyclable material, reducing environmental impact.
The juice is low in calories – about 40 kcal per 100 ml.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Fruit polyphenols help neutralize free radicals and support heart health.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The juice is mostly water, contributing to the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber from the fruits promotes normal bowel function.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: Absence of added sugar makes the juice suitable for those monitoring blood glucose levels.

items.title: Fruit allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to specific fruits used in the blend.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity may irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcer disease.

items.title: Natural sugar content
items.content: Although no sugar is added, the juice contains natural sugars, which should be considered by diabetics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The juice can be enjoyed chilled as a refreshing drink, used in smoothies, cocktails, or culinary recipes that call for a fruity note.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Stew, vegetable is a blend of various vegetables cooked slowly in a small amount of liquid. Typical ingredients include carrots, potatoes, onions, celery, bell peppers and tomatoes. The vegetables retain most of their nutrients, and the soft texture makes them easy to eat at any age.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stewed vegetables are often used as a base for soups and ragouts in many traditional cuisines.
Slow cooking enhances the natural sweetness of the vegetables.
Combining several vegetable types increases the bioavailability of certain vitamins, such as vitamin C and carotenoids.
Stewed vegetables keep well in the refrigerator for up to 5 days and can be frozen for up to 3 months without loss of flavor.
In some cultures, stewed vegetables are served cold as a salad.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Provides vitamins A, C, K and B‑complex, which support immunity, vision and metabolism.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Stewed vegetables contain virtually no saturated fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Lycopene, beta‑carotene and other phytochemicals protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium helps maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Allergy to individual vegetables
items.content: Some people may be allergic to tomatoes, peppers or celery.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding salt or ready‑made sauces can raise sodium levels, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage above 4 °C can allow pathogenic bacteria to grow.

items.title: Nutrient interactions
items.content: Large amounts of vegetables may reduce iron absorption from plant sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stewed vegetables can be served as a side dish, added to soups, ragouts, pasta, or used as a sandwich filling. They reheat easily in the microwave or on the stove and can be incorporated into cold salads after cooling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator at +4 °C for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Discard if you notice off‑odors, mold or spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet and sour pork is a classic Chinese dish featuring bite‑size pieces of pork that are deep‑fried until crisp and then tossed in a glossy sauce made from vinegar, sugar, soy sauce, tomato paste, and spices. The result is a crunchy exterior with a bright balance of tangy and sweet flavors.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in Canton in the 19th century and quickly spread throughout Asia.
Traditional sauce is made with rice vinegar, sugar, soy sauce, tomato paste, and sometimes pineapple juice.
Pork is often coated in cornstarch or potato starch before frying to achieve a crisp crust.
In the United States the dish is commonly served with pineapple chunks and bell peppers, although they are not part of the original recipe.
Sweet and sour pork is often considered a comfort food in Chinese restaurants because of its bold flavor and quick preparation.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Pork provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish contains B1, B2, and B6 vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Pork supplies iron, zinc, and selenium, important for immune function and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants in the sauce
items.content: Tomatoes and vinegar contribute lycopene and polyphenols with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and modest fat helps maintain fullness longer.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and the prepared sauce can add a lot of salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Added sugar raises the calorie count and may affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Trans fats from frying
items.content: Deep‑frying can generate trans fats; using a high‑smoke‑point oil reduces this risk.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: People allergic to soy should substitute soy sauce with a soy‑free alternative.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve sweet and sour pork hot, typically over steamed rice or noodles. Add fresh vegetables such as bell peppers or pineapple for texture contrast. Garnish with sliced green onions or toasted sesame seeds.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. Reheat in a skillet to retain crispness. Do not freeze already fried pieces, as the texture may become soggy.
